extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write mathematical proofs (introductory proofs/discrete math)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and proving mathematical statements (direct, contrapositive, contradiction proofs), plus stylistic rules for clear mathematical exposition aimed at beginning proof writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional 'If P, then Q', assume P is true and use logic/definitions to deduce Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline for Direct Proof: Proposition If P, then Q. Proof. Suppose P. Therefore Q. (Use definitions and algebraic manipulation as appropriate.) Examples show using case analysis when needed (split depending on parity, sign, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating similar cases / use of 'Without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more cases are nearly identical, you may present just one case and indicate the others are analogous using the phrase 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal WLOG when the remaining cases are 'entirely alike except for order'. Avoid abbreviating as 'WLOG' in formal writing; for transparency, beginners are advised to write out all cases even if similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive proof (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' prove the logically equivalent statement '~Q => ~P' by assuming ~Q and deducing ~P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline for Contrapositive Proof: Proposition If P, then Q. Proof. Suppose ~Q. Therefore ~P. Use negation techniques (DeMorgan's Laws, etc.) when working with ~P and ~Q. The first line typically is 'Suppose Q is not true.' and the last line 'Therefore P is not true.' Examples demonstrate contrapositive can be easier than direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negation rules (DeMorgan etc.) when proving contrapositives and contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with negated statements (~P, ~Q or combinations), apply formal negation laws (e.g., DeMorgan's Law) to transform complex negations into usable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To negate '5|x and 5|y' use DeMorgan to get '5|x or 5|y' when forming contrapositives. Consider separate subcases produced by DeMorgan's transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement P, assume its negation ~P and deduce a contradiction (some C and ~C). Conclude P must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline for Proof by Contradiction: Proposition P. Proof. Suppose ~P. Therefore C and ~C. Any clearly false statement qualifies as a contradiction (e.g., '1 is even', '4|2'). You may not know the contradiction C initially — derive consequences of ~P until a contradiction appears. Classic examples: irrationality of sqrt(2), infinitude of primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving conditional statements by contradiction (specialized outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' by contradiction, assume P and ~Q (since ~(P=>Q) is equivalent to P and ~Q) and deduce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: Proposition If P, then Q. Proof. Suppose P and ~Q. Therefore C and ~C. Example shows assuming P and ~Q can yield a direct contradiction (e.g., parity arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct/contrapositive over contradiction when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof by contradiction only when direct or contrapositive approaches do not seem to work; contradiction proofs often hide simpler contrapositive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: If a contradiction proof contains a step that assumes ~Q and deduces ~P, prefer rewriting as a contrapositive proof for clarity and efficiency. Examples demonstrate converting a contradiction proof into a contrapositive proof reduces redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining techniques / proofs within proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: It's acceptable and often necessary to combine proof techniques: start with one method (e.g., direct) and use another (contradiction or contrapositive) inside to prove an auxiliary claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs can contain nested proofs; e.g., to show r/√2 is irrational one uses direct proof overall and an inner proof by contradiction. Label inner proofs clearly and justify transitions between methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never begin a sentence with a mathematical symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should begin with words (capital letters); starting with a symbol can cause ambiguity due to case-sensitivity of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'x is an integer...' (bad). Better: 'Since x is an integer, ...' Provide examples of bad vs good usage. This avoids ambiguous capitalization issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: End each sentence with a period (punctuate mathematical statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematical statements (equations, inequalities, etc.) like English phrases and use normal punctuation; end sentences with periods even when they end with a mathematical expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ensure displayed or inline math ends with appropriate punctuation. This improves readability and grammatical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate mathematical symbols and expressions with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words to separate expressions so distinct parts do not appear to merge together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'Since x^2 - 1 = 0, x = 1 or x = -1.' (ambiguous). Better: 'Since x^2 - 1 = 0, it follows that x = 1 or x = -1.' Also: 'Unlike A∪B, A∩B equals 0' should be 'Unlike A∪B, the set A∩B equals 0.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of symbols as words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols such as =, <, ∈, etc., are not words and should not be used in place of their verbal equivalents in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'Since the two sets are =, ...' Better: 'Since the two sets are equal, ...' Do not write 'The empty set is a ⊂ of every set.' Use words: 'subset'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce extra notation or variable names when they do not aid clarity; keep writing as simple as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'No set X has negative cardinality.' Better: 'No set has negative cardinality.' Avoid cluttering text with irrelevant symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person plural ('we') in mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt 'we' and 'us' rather than 'I', 'you' or 'me' to create a conversational guiding tone in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a stylistic convention in mathematical exposition that helps guide the reader through reasoning steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions as they make writing more lively and clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'The value x = 3 is obtained through the division of both sides by 5.' Better: 'Dividing both sides by 5, we get x = 3.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain each new symbol when introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a new symbol or variable is introduced in a proof, explicitly state its meaning or existence (e.g., 'there exists an integer c such that...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'Since a|b, it follows that b = ac.' (bad because c not introduced). Better: 'Since a|b, it follows that b = ac for some integer c.' This prevents readers from backtracking to find where a symbol came from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous pronouns (watch out for 'it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'it' when its antecedent could be unclear; replace 'it' with the explicit noun when confusion is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'Since X ⊂ Y, and |X| < |X|, we see that it is not empty.' Clarify which set 'it' refers to: 'we see that Y is not empty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with conjunctions like 'since', 'because', 'so' (they assert antecedent truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'since', 'because', 'so' assert that the preceding premise is true, not just that it implies another statement; use them only when the premise is indeed assumed or established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Using 'so' can incorrectly assert membership. Wrong: 'x ∈ N, so x ∈ Z' vs correct use: ensure the premise is actually given/true before using these conjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'thus', 'hence', 'therefore', 'consequently' only for logical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve these adverbs for statements that truly follow logically from previous lines; ensure the implication is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'Therefore 2k + 1.' (incomplete). Better: 'Therefore a = 2k + 1.' Make sure the conclusion is explicit and justified.
